content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents Abductive DETR which employs extra learnable embeddings and visual features as inputs of the transformer encoder and matches decoded queries to boxes via abductive matching. Particularly, two additional region attributes: number and class of objects,  are incorporated into the region tokens to form the encodings with the spatial distribution of objects. In the decoding of object queries, a query can concentrate on a certain region rather than glob the targets in the whole image for efficient matching. In experiments, the proposed approach was evaluated on the benchmark MS COCO dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

- Works on the problem of decoding efficiency in DETR: grounding queries onto image regions 

- Employs extra learnable embeddings and visual features as inputs of the transformer encoder for efficient matching


Weaknesses

- Important baselines are missing. Some important baselines (e.g., DINO, Zhang et al. ECCV 2022) are not included in the paper. The paper only compares with a partial list of the state-of-the-art approaches but does not contain the most recent work. The conclusion seems unjustified without a comprehensive comparison with respect to all of the state-of-the-art approaches.

- Experiments are lacking. 

(a) The paper claims that the proposed Abductive DETR arrives at convergence much faster. But no experiments regarding the convergence of the learning process of Abductive DETR are included.

(b) The learning of region tokens is not clear. Extra learnable embeddings and visual features are dispensable inputs to the proposed approach. But there is not even a sentence regarding the module for learning the embeddings. Also, there is no analysis of the cases when the two additional region attributes are not accurate.

(c) Latency comparisons are missing. The extra learnable embeddings will definitely introduce additional runtime overhead even though the proposed approach uses way fewer object queries. It would be better to include a comparison of FPS.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The author(s) promised to release the code in the future for reproducibility but a link to the implementation is not included in the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper studies an interesting problem in the framework of DETR that suffers from limited novelty, lacking experiments, and incomplete comparisons.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work introduces Abductive DETR, which aims to improve upon the DETR style methods by investigating the query generation as well as the loss-matching process. The work identifies two bottlenecks of the DETR: poor object queries and inefficient assignments using Hungarian Matching. The work proposes to generate learned queries which use image region attributes number and class of objects. The proposed updated matching explicitly minimizes an uncertainty and redundancy term. The authors evaluate their results on the COCO dataset and show strong performance over a series of DETR-styled baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
This work proposes a simple and elegant solution to the query generation problem faced in DETR-style methods. The strongest point of this work is its extensive experiment section. The ablation section is complete, and justifies each of the components in the method. The authors also compare Abductive DETR to a strong set of baselines, which – to the best of my knowledge – is comprehensive. In particular, it compares favorably against a majority of DETR-styled models and their variants (Table 2), although DN-DETR in many settings is comparable. 

It is very nice to see that this method utilizes much fewer queries, and has a significant speedup over other methods (“27 x faster”); however, I am not seeing this reflected in Table 2, under the “GFLOPs” column. Should I be looking at another table regarding this?

**Weaknesses**
The work is quite difficult to read, and there appears to be a few equations that are unnecessary and confusing. This is a problem in Section 4 especially. However, the diagrams provided help offer clarity; the writing should reflect the diagrams more.
Abductive DETR builds on top of DETR, and provides a solution. This provides an incremental improvement over the previous works (ie, works that aim to generate better queries and matches). However, the experimental results seem strong, and the proposed solution is simple and, if the code is released, can be a large contribution to the community. 
There appears to be a few claims that are not backed up by the experimental results. For example, in the abstract: “...only 2 epochs to achieve the 98.7% accuracy of predicting the number of objects”.

**Miscellaneous**
Introduction, P2: Besides, some works → Some works/Other works
Introduction, P3: the limitations of training a DETR are still suffering from the dilemma → training a DETR are still suffering from the dilemma
Introduction, P3: which are of significance → which significantly [affect convergence]
Section 4.1: Foal Loss → Focal Loss
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors mention in the work that the code will be released soon, which aids in reproducibility. 
There are some elements of the work that make it difficult to read. Some of the equations are redundant and make the work difficult to read. For example, Equation 1 is unnecessary and confuses the reader. Expressing it more clearly or removing it altogether and replacing it with a description would improve the readability. Equation 2 is unnecessary as well; the general audience is aware of what the mean squared error is (and regression in general). However, the figures provided help clarify the work (most notably Figure 2). A better intuitive explanation of equations 5, 6 would help make the paper more clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the work is quite difficult to read; however, the method proposed is simple and yields strong performance. There are a few claims that the authors make in the work that are not explicitly shown in the experiments; if they are true, it would make the work very strong. As it stands, I would be willing to increase my rating if the issues of unbacked claims and clarity are addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an Abductive DETR, which tackles the uncertainty issue of Hungarian matching in DETR by (1) minimizing the uncertainty for different assignments that correspond to similar box losses and (2) reducing the redundant assignments across training epochs. The general idea is neat and novel, and the experimental results are promising.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
    + A novel and interesting perspective for DETR-based object detection. 
    + Promising results on the COCO dataset.

Weaknesses:

    - There should be an ablation study for the loss functions of uncertainty and redundancy. The current version cannot reflect the importance of the main design in the proposed method. 

    - The number of queries in the proposed method is not clear. The authors said that the proposed method uses less than 100 queries in their experiments, so, how many queries were used? In my understanding, there should be 100 queries but some of the queries are not activated during training. Is my understanding correct? 

    - In the proposed method, the authors only take the box losses into account for the modeling. How would it be if the classification losses were taken into account?

    - In the introduction, the sentence "it proves that...." for the 3rd contribution is not complete.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written and presents a novel perspective for DETR-based object detection. The presented method is new and effective to improve the performance of object detection.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper addressed an important problem of the matching uncertainty in DETR. The presented method is novel, elegant and effective, which is also well-supported by the experimental results.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Despite my best efforts, I could not understand what the contributions the authors claim are, and how the proposed method works. It looks like the authors make two modifications to DETR:
- they somehow modify the assignment step between the predicted bounding boxes are their probabilities
- looks like they make a similar modification as DAB-DETR, by adding learnable anchors. I could not understand how it works.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I could not understand what are the claimed contributions of the paper. They are formulated vaguely with unexplained terms and concepts, and without connecting to prior work. It is not clear how the claimed contributions are beneficial for the scientific community.

Contribution 1:
“successfully establishes a reliable learning representations in the pixel space with region tokens from representation space to concentrate on the pre-definite attributes.”
- what is learning representations in pixel space?
- what are the “region tokens”?
- what are the “pre-definite attributes”?
- what does it mean “to concentrate on the pre-definite attributes” ? how is it proven?
Contribution 2:
“ we are the first to propose abductive costs to compensate these disadvantages, which reveals that abductive-
aware maximum-weights matching is better for training a detector”
- what are the “abductive costs”?
- what are the disadvantages?
- what does it mean to be “abductive-aware” ?
- what is “maximum-weights matching”
- saying that something is better can be subjective. Please formulate this clearly specifying the aspect in which it is better, for example, simplicity, traning time, computation efficiency.
Contribution 3
This contribution is composed of multiple statements not making up a contribution. It ends with abruptly ending “It proves that” sentence. What does it prove?
“They takes only 2 epochs to achieve 98.7% accuracy for precisely predicting the number of objects”
Why is it important to correctly predict the number of objects? How does it connect to prior work?

From the empirical results, it looks like the method yields similar benchmark numbers to other DETR modifications, or marginally better. The authors claim that the method is 27 times faster in the matching step, but there is no empirical evidence on this, on the setup and how to reproduce this. It is not clear why the matching step needs to be faster, and what fraction of training it takes.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very hard to understand. One example:
“ The matching costs just formulate the single-round objective, and the comprehensive matching costs are neither scheduled nor optimized in the whole training process, which brings redundancy.”
- what are the matching costs the authors refer to? what does it mean for matching costs to be comprehensive
- what is a “single-round objective” ?
- how can matching costs be scheduled?

As it is very difficult to read and understand the paper, it would also be difficult to reproduce the results.

The figures in the draft are confusing. Figure 2 contradicts Algorithm 1 in how the method works.
content.summary_of_the_review: I suggest strong reject, there is a lot of work needed to be done on the paper: to formulate the contributions, to connect them with empirical claims, and improve readability.

content.title: Guide Detectors in Pixel Space with Global Positioning and Abductive Matching
content.abstract: End-to-End object Detector ensembles prior knowledge in a concise framework. DETR (DEtection TRansformer) contains two steps: Learn object queries in the representation space and match the queries with boxes in the pixel space. The ambiguity of object queries in DETR lead to an uncertain assignment in the Hungarian Matching. The formulation loss in the pixel space will in turn affect the learning representations. Therefore, we propose the Abductive DETR, which learns object queries in the representation space with global positioning in the pixel space and matches object queries in the pixel space with the abductive awareness from the representation space.  Experimentally, Abductive DETR can be transferred to other DETR-variants methods and achieves a satisfactory improvement. And it takes only 2 epochs to achieve the 98.7% accuracy of predicting the number of objects. Compared with other state-of-the-art methods on the MS COCO dataset, Abductive DETR also achieves outstanding performance and arrives at convergence much faster. Our code will be made publicly available soon.
